sentences.text: The genus name Incisivosaurus highlights the dinosaur's prominent, rodent-like front teeth which display wear patterns typical of plant-eaters.
A 2004 study noted the skull possessed a long snout comprising about half the total length, a slender lower jaw with a long opening, and distinctive large, flattened front teeth.
The skull averages about 10 centimeters in length and preserves the most complete dentition known for an oviraptorosaurian.
The total body length of this animal is estimated to be less than one meter.
Two juvenile feathered specimens from 2010 showed long symmetrical vaned feathers on the hands and tails, with the rest of the body covered in downy feathers.
The most significant and unusual feature of this dinosaur is its apparent adaptation to a herbivorous or omnivorous lifestyle.
The first Incisivosaurus specimen, a skull named IVPP V13326, was described by Xu et al. in 2002 from the Barremian stage of the Yixian Formation in western Liaoning Province, China.
The first specimen was discovered in 2002 in the lowest riverbed layer of the Yixian Formation near Sihetun, close to Beipiao in western Liaoning province.
The species was named for its prominent front teeth resembling those of rodents, showing wear patterns common in plant-eating dinosaurs.
The species name honors Dr. Jacques Gauthier, a pioneer in phylogeny, a method of classification.
Incisivosaurus was a small, probably herbivorous theropod dinosaur from the early Cretaceous Period of what is now China.
It is assumed that Incisivosaurus had feathers like other maniraptorans and may have secondarily lost the ability to fly.
Despite unique traits, Incisivosaurus shared many features with typical oviraptorosaurs, allowing its classification within that group.
In a weighted cladogram, Incisivosaurus became the sister taxon to Protarchaeopteryx, representing the most primitive group of oviraptorosaurs.
It is possible that Incisivosaurus is a synonym of Protarchaeopteryx, though more fossil specimens are needed before the two can be directly compared.
Incisivosaurus lived during the early Cretaceous Period, approximately 128 million years ago in the Barremian stage, in what is now Asia.
Incisivosaurus lived from the Barremian to the Albian stages, between 125.77 and 100.5 million years ago.

Feather development specialist Richard Prum disputed the interpretation that feather structures changed with age, suggesting instead that the ribbon-like structures represented feathers in the process of moulting.
Xu et al. (2010) rebutted the moulting hypothesis, arguing the evidence was problematic due to the absence of previous-generation feathers and that the structure was too large to be a pin feather.
In the third episode of the ITV series Prehistoric Park, it is theorized that Incisivosaurus used its feathered wings for display and that they would have been used for flight in the past.
